'''Muzaffer Atac''' (''Ataç'', 24 August 1933 – 7 December 2010) was a Turkish-American physicist who was one of the founding scientists of Fermilab and performed important work with [[Visible-light photon counter|visible light photon counters]] and other [[particle detector|detectors]] for [[particle physics]].<ref name="Fermilab">{{cite web |url = http://history.fnal.gov/findingaids/Atac_ibatf2012006.html#d0e87/ |title = Finding Aid to the Muzaffer Atac Papers |publisher = Fermilab History and Archives Project, Fermi National Accelerator Laboratory |date = 2013 |accessdate= 13 February 2013 }}</ref>

==Early life and career==

Muzaffer Atac was born on August 24, 1933, in [[Kemaliye]], a rural town in [[Turkey]]. He attended high school in [[Ankara]], Turkey<ref name="obit">{{cite news |title=Muzaffer Atac, 1931-2010 |author=Bob Goldsborough |url=https://www.chicagotribune.com/2010/12/16/muzaffer-atac-1931-2010/ |newspaper=Chicago Tribune |date=16 December 2010 |access-date=13 February 2013}}</ref> and received his BS in physics from [[Ankara University]] in 1957.<ref name="Fermilab"/> Atac married his wife, Ayfer Temiztaş,<ref name="Fermilab"/> on March 21, 1958.<ref name="obit"/> They had three children.<ref name="Fermilab"/>

From 1959 to 1961, Atac was employed by the Minerals Searching and Investigating Institute in Ankara.<ref name="Fermilab"/> In January 1961,<ref name="obit"/> Atac moved to the United States to study physics at the [[University of Illinois at Urbana–Champaign|University of Illinois]] with the support of a [[NATO]] fellowship. He received his MS in physics from this institution in 1963. Atac completed his PhD thesis "Time Reversal Violation in Electromagnetic Interactions" under the supervision of [[Hans Frauenfelder]] at the University of Illinois.<ref name="Fermilab"/> He returned to [[Ankara University]] for eight months as part of his PhD work<ref name="obit"/> and received his PhD degree from Ankara University.<ref name="Fermilab"/>

==Fermilab and later career==

On September 3, 1968, Atac began working for the [[United States Department of Energy]]'s National Accelerator Laboratory, which would later become [[Fermilab]]. Atac moved to [[Wheaton, Illinois]], in January 1971, where he would remain for the rest of his life.<ref name="Fermilab"/>

While at Fermilab, Atac performed groundbreaking work with gas calorimeters, wire drift chambers, and high sensitivity solid state photon detectors, and he received several patents for his work.<ref name="Fermilab"/> He later became interested in applications of particle detectors in the medical field<ref name="obit"/> and did work in medical imaging and the early detection of breast cancer. His work in this area produced several patented biomedical imaging devices. Atac served as head of Fermilab’s detector development group from 1972 until 1978, when he joined the [[Collider Detector at Fermilab]] (CDF) experiment. He was one of the first three scientists involved in this experiment, and he remained with CDF until 1997.<ref name="Fermilab"/> Beginning in 1988, he worked on the development of solid state [[photomultiplier]]s and [[Visible-light photon counter|visible light photon counters]] with [[Rockwell International]]. In 1989, he became an adjunct professor of physics at the [[University of California, Los Angeles]], and he became an adjunct professor at the [[University of Texas at Dallas]] in 1990. He began working on cancer research at the [[University of California, Irvine]] in 1996. Beginning in 1995, Atac worked on developing a Silicon Pixels Vertex Tracking System for the [[Compact Muon Solenoid]] (CMS) experiment at [[CERN]]'s [[Large Hadron Collider]].<ref name="Fermilab"/> Atac was author or co-author on over 500 publications.<ref name="inspire">{{cite web |url=http://inspirehep.net/author/M.Atac.1/ |title=Atac, Muzaffer publication list |work=INSPIRE |accessdate=13 February 2013}}</ref>

Atac retired from Fermilab in June 2008 and died in his home on December 7, 2010.<ref name="obit"/>
